Variegated means marked by patches, streaks, or spots of different colors in an irregular, natural-looking way — or, more broadly, having a rich and interesting variety of different things.

Those are the two main senses of the word, and both share the same underlying soul: the idea of many different things existing together in a beautifully uneven, non-uniform way.
Sense 1: The Visual Meaning (Colors and Patterns)

This is the most common and most literal use of the word.

When something is variegated, it is not a single, flat color. It has two or more colors appearing together in irregular, naturally distributed patches or streaks. The key word here is irregular — the colors are not neatly arranged in a geometric pattern like stripes or polka dots. Instead, they appear in a more organic, unplanned, almost unpredictable way — the way nature tends to do things.

The classic example is a variegated plant leaf. Imagine a houseplant whose leaves are not fully green. Instead, some parts of each leaf are green, other parts are creamy white, and yet other parts are pale yellow — all mixed together in an uneven, flowing pattern. That leaf is variegated. Gardeners and botanists use this word constantly.

Other visual examples:

A variegated stone is one that has swirls and patches of brown, white, and gray running through it — like marble.

A variegated thread used in knitting or weaving changes color gradually as you go, so the finished fabric comes out with a rich, multi-colored, unpatterned look.

A variegated sky at sunset — streaked with pink, orange, purple, and gold — could fairly be called variegated.

The critical distinction from similar words: "multicolored" simply means having many colors. "Variegated" goes one step further — it tells you that those colors appear in an irregular, patchwork, naturally distributed way, not in a neat or planned arrangement. It also carries a sense of visual richness that plain "multicolored" does not.
Sense 2: The Figurative Meaning (Variety and Diversity)

In its second, more abstract sense, variegated simply means full of variety; diverse; made up of many different kinds of things.

Here, you are not talking about literal colors. You are using the image of a colorful, patchy, richly mixed thing as a metaphor for anything that has a lot of different elements in it.

A variegated career = a career that has included many different kinds of jobs, roles, and experiences — not a single narrow path.

A variegated literary tradition = a body of literature with many different styles, voices, and forms.

A variegated cityscape = a city that looks and feels very different from block to block — old buildings next to modern ones, quiet parks next to busy markets, wealthy neighborhoods next to humble ones.

A variegated education = schooling that covered a wide range of subjects and experiences.

In this sense, variegated is close in meaning to words like "diverse," "multifaceted," or "rich in variety." But variegated often suggests something more vivid and visually imaginative than those words — it carries the picture of that colorful, patchy leaf in your mind even when you're using it to describe something non-visual.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Variegated almost always carries a positive or neutral connotation. When you call something variegated, you are usually suggesting that its variety is a good thing — that the mix of colors, textures, or experiences makes it more interesting, richer, and more beautiful than it would be if it were plain and uniform.

It is the opposite of monotonous. It is the opposite of dull, flat, and same.

This is a formal and literary word. You would not say it in casual, everyday conversation — it would sound out of place. Instead, you would find it in well-crafted writing, academic texts, nature writing, botanical descriptions, and literary prose. When a writer chooses the word "variegated" over "colorful" or "diverse," they are reaching for a word with more precision, more elegance, and more texture.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Colorful just means bright and vivid in color. It doesn't say anything about the pattern or distribution. A solid red car is colorful. It is not variegated.

Multicolored means having more than one color, but says nothing about the pattern being irregular or organic. A rainbow is multicolored; it is not usually called variegated because its colors appear in a regular, ordered arc.

Mottled means blotched or spotted with color in an irregular way — similar to variegated, but mottled often implies something that looks a bit rough, diseased, or unattractive (like mottled skin). Variegated does not carry that negative sense.

Dappled refers specifically to patches of light and shadow, or soft spots of color — often used for sunlight filtering through leaves. It is narrower than variegated.

Varied and diverse are the closest to variegated in the figurative sense, but they are plainer and less vivid. Variegated suggests a richer, more visually striking kind of variety.

If you had to boil it down to one sentence: variegated means richly mixed with different colors or kinds of things, in an irregular, naturally distributed, interesting way.

Whether someone is describing the leaves of a tropical plant, the surface of an ancient stone, a sweeping landscape, or a long and eventful life — when they reach for the word "variegated," they are saying: this is not plain, not uniform, not monotonous. It is alive with variety, and that variety is something worth noticing.
